body_markdown:
Property managers wear many hats. They manage budgets, oversee operations, respond to residents, support their teams, and keep properties running smoothly. But one of their most important responsibilities often gets less attention: hiring the people who will help them do it all.


The ability to identify the right candidate, ask meaningful questions, evaluate potential, and create a positive candidate experience directly impacts a property's performance. A strong hire can strengthen a team, improve resident experiences, and reduce turnover. A poor fit can create additional work for an already stretched property manager and affect the rest of the team.


For property managers, becoming a better interviewer means becoming a more intentional leader.


##


**Start With the Role, Not the Resume**


One of the easiest ways to improve an interview is to clarify what you're actually hiring for and how you define success before the conversation begins.


A resume can tell you where someone has worked and what responsibilities they've had, but it doesn't necessarily tell you whether they'll succeed at your property. Before interviewing candidates, think beyond the job description. What does this position actually require on a day-to-day basis? What challenges will this person face? Which skills can be taught, and which qualities are essential from day one?


For example, a candidate may have impressive industry experience, but if the role requires constant resident interaction, adaptability, and the ability to stay composed during difficult conversations, those qualities should be part of the interview, not an afterthought.


The best hiring decisions start with a clear definition of success.


##


**Ask Questions That Reveal How Someone Thinks**


Good interview questions reveal how candidates approach problems, communicate, make decisions, and respond when things don't go according to plan.


Instead of asking whether someone has performed a particular task, ask them to explain how they handled a real situation. How did they respond to an upset resident? What did they do when they had competing priorities? How did they handle a mistake?


These questions give property managers a better understanding of how candidates operate. They're also particularly valuable in property management, where every day can bring unexpected challenges. Technical knowledge matters, but so do judgment, communication, problem-solving, and emotional intelligence.


##


**Look for Potential, Not Just Experience**


Experience is important, but it shouldn't be the only measure of a strong candidate.


Property managers sometimes feel pressure to find someone who can step into a role and immediately know everything. In reality, the strongest candidate may be someone who has the right foundation, attitude, and ability to learn—even if they don't check every box on the job description.


Consider how a candidate responds when they don't know something. Are they curious? Do they ask thoughtful questions? Can they describe how they've learned new skills in the past? Do they take ownership when discussing mistakes?


A candidate's capacity to learn and grow can be just as valuable as the experience they already have.


##


**Pay Attention to the Candidate Experience**


An interview isn't a one-way evaluation. Candidates are evaluating the property, the company, and the leadership team, as well.


Property managers should remember that the way they conduct an interview communicates what it might be like to work for them. Showing up prepared, respecting the candidate's time, explaining the role honestly, and creating space for questions can make a meaningful difference.


This is particularly important in a competitive hiring environment. A candidate who feels ignored, rushed, or unclear about the opportunity may decide the position isn't right for them, even if they were initially excited about it.


A strong candidate experience doesn't require an elaborate process. It requires communication, preparation, and respect.


##


**Don't Let "Gut Feeling" Make the Decision**


Leaders naturally develop instincts about people. Sometimes those instincts are valuable. But relying too heavily on a gut feeling can introduce bias into the hiring process.


A candidate who reminds you of a great employee you once had may feel like an obvious fit. Another candidate may have a personality that immediately clicks with you. Neither should be the sole reason for making a hiring decision.


Instead, use consistent questions and evaluation criteria for every candidate. Compare candidates against the requirements of the role rather than against each other or your personal preferences.


##


**Treat the Interview as the Beginning of Leadership**


The expectations established during the interview should carry into onboarding, training, coaching, and ongoing performance conversations. If you tell a candidate that communication, accountability, or resident service are important during the interview, those qualities should remain part of the employee's experience once they're on the team.


Property managers who approach hiring this way aren't simply filling open positions. They're building teams intentionally. And that can have a ripple effect across the entire property.


##


**Better Interviews Can Lead to Better Teams**


Property management is a people-driven business. The strength of a property team influences everything from daily operations to resident satisfaction. When property managers become more thoughtful and effective interviewers, they give themselves a better opportunity to build teams that can handle the demands of the job.


That doesn't mean every hire will be perfect. But a more intentional interview process can help property managers make informed decisions, recognize potential, reduce hiring mistakes, and create a stronger candidate experience along the way.
